sections.title: AI agent or AI automation workflow?

blocks.heading: AI automation workflow ($15,000–$60,000)
paragraphs: A pre-defined sequence of steps with fixed decision logic. It handles variable inputs such as documents and unstructured text but follows a fixed process path — lower cost and predictable behaviour. Best for document processing, email triage, report generation and data extraction.

blocks.heading: AI agent ($45,000–$200,000+)
paragraphs: Dynamically decides which steps to take based on intermediate results and can handle situations the developer did not anticipate. It costs more and needs more reliability engineering, but suits open-ended work such as research, complex customer-service cases and multi-step resolution.

blocks.heading: What makes agents expensive to get right
paragraphs: Each tool integration needs authentication, rate limiting, retries and tests. Reliability engineering — step validation, error classification and fallback behaviour — adds 20–35% to scope. Approval workflows, memory and security hardening are scoped explicitly so there are no surprises.

items.question: What's the minimum budget for a useful AI agent?
items.answer: $45,000 for a single agent with a defined tool set and well-scoped workflow. Simpler automation workflows that don't need adaptive decision-making are achievable for $15,000–$30,000.

items.question: How long does AI agent development take?
items.answer: 12–40 weeks depending on complexity. Single-agent: 12–24 weeks. Multi-agent enterprise platform: 24–40 weeks.

items.question: What frameworks do you use?
items.answer: LangGraph for stateful multi-step agents, LangChain agents, AutoGen for multi-agent coordination, and custom orchestration where specific reliability requirements call for it. Framework choice follows the agent's complexity.

items.question: Can you build an agent that works with Salesforce, SAP or ServiceNow?
items.answer: Yes — CRM and ERP integration is one of the most common agent tool types. We scope the specific API capabilities needed during discovery.

items.question: How do you test that an agent works before deployment?
items.answer: With a task-completion test suite: representative tasks with defined success criteria, evaluated for end-to-end completion rate, step accuracy, error handling and prompt-injection resistance.

items.question: What's the difference between a single agent and a multi-agent system?
items.answer: A single agent performs all tasks with its own tool set. A multi-agent system uses a supervisor agent that decomposes tasks and delegates to specialist agents. Multi-agent systems cost 2–3x more but handle significantly more complex work.
